findings.claim: Item /74 states the curve case as 'only finitely many curves of a given genus' with good reduction outside S. That is false for genus 1. For example, take K = ℚ, E = X_0(11) (E(ℚ) finite, Ш(E) finite) and S = {11, p}. Genus-one curves with Jacobian E and good reduction outside S are the classes in H¹(ℚ,E) that are trivial at every v ∉ S. A torsor with good reduction at v has a ℚ_v-point by Lang's theorem and Hensel. Cassels' sequence H¹(ℚ,E) → ⊕_v H¹(ℚ_v,E) → (E(ℚ)^∧)^* has finite cokernel, and H¹(ℚ_p,E) ≅ E(ℚ_p)^∨ ⊇ ℚ_p/ℤ_p is infinite, so there are infinitely many such classes. Since Aut(E) is finite, they give infinitely many isomorphism classes of curves. Faltings' theorem and the planned R28.5 node both require genus ≥ 2, and only that case is used: a smooth curve representing an ample ϕ on an abelian surface has genus 1 + ϕ²/2 ≥ 2. Separately, the planned owner is mis-cited. The curve statement is the R28.5 packet node, and RP.4 plans the Parshin reduction to Mordell, not this statement. The note also overstates the paper: the paper says only that 'there does not seem to be any logical relation', and the note turns that into 'logically independent' and 'there is no nonconstant map'. Also: Item /74 says both halves are planned: Shafarevich finiteness for abelian varieties, and 'only finitely many curves of a given genus' with good reduction outside S. findings.claim: The acceptance test 'the theta divisor of a Jacobian, where the convolution group is the classical one of Krämer–Weissauer' is wrong. Krämer–Weissauer's classical result ([46]) is for the theta divisor of a generic principally polarized abelian variety. For a Jacobian, Θ is the (g−1)-st convolution power of the curve, so its group acts through a wedge power: case (3) of Lemma 3.10, not the standard representation. Moreover, the theta divisor of a Jacobian of genus g ≥ 4 is singular (by the Riemann singularity theorem, Sing Θ ⊇ W¹_{g−1}, which is nonempty for g ≥ 4), so it lies outside Theorem 3.5, which is about smooth H. A worker checking Theorem 3.5 on this test would find a contradiction.

findings.claim: The proof of Theorem 9.2 asserts that, by properness, every S-integral point of Hilb lifts to an S-integral point of the resolution 𝒳. That is false: a proper birational morphism need not be surjective on rational points. Take the blow-up of the vertex of the cone over a conic without ℚ-points; the vertex is a ℚ-point whose exceptional fibre has no ℚ-point. The conclusion the proof needs, that the integral points of 𝒳 are Zariski dense, still holds. X_sing is an irreducible component of the closure, so the integral points it contains that lie in the dense open U over which X → X_sing is an isomorphism are dense in X_sing. Those points lift to X(ℚ), and then to 𝒳(ℤ[1/S′]) by the valuative criterion. /59 does not record this step.
findings.evidence: p. 86: 'Now, by properness, every S-integral point of Hilb lifts to an S-integral point of 𝒳, so by construction the S-integral points are Zariski dense in 𝒳.'
findings.fix: Add a sourceIssue: 'Proof of Theorem 9.2 (p. 86): integral points need not lift through the resolution X → X_sing. Repair: the integral points of X_sing in the open U ⊆ X_sing over which X → X_sing is an isomorphism are Zariski dense in X_sing (X_sing is irreducible and is a component of the closure). They lift to X(ℚ), and by the valuative criterion for the proper 𝒳 → Res Hilb they extend to 𝒳(ℤ[1/S′]), so 𝒳(ℤ[1/S′]) is Zariski dense in X.' findings.claim: The proof of Lemma 8.14 applies Lemma 8.13 to ψ = Ad(φ) on the unipotent radical U of P. But ψ^r = Ad(φ^r) with φ^r ∈ M semisimple, and this is not the identity on U in general, so the hypothesis ψ^r = id_U of Lemma 8.13 fails. The gap is repairable. From u·ψ(u)⋯ψ^{r−1}(u) = 1, applying ψ gives ψ^r(u) = u, so u lies in U' := Z_U(φ^r). This is a ψ-stable unipotent subgroup on which ψ^r = id. Lemma 8.13 applied to U' gives u = v^{−1}ψ(v) with v ∈ U'. Lemma 8.14 lies on the main chain (8.14 → 8.15 → 8.16 → 8.17).

findings.claim: The proof of Theorem 9.6 uses more than Faltings's theorem, and /4 records none of it and cross-references nothing (planned []). B.3–B.5 and B.9 write E(n,q) for A(n,q), and B.5 cites E(2,q) where A(3,q) is meant. B.4 writes m_S(w) for m_H(w) and 'Σ_i m_S(i) equal to kw and kw+1' for Σ_i i·m_S(i). B.9, case (0, m−3, 3, 0, 0): all four right-hand sides are printed as dE(4,0). B.23: 'A(n,4) ≥ N(m^b_4)/N(m^b_1)' should be N(m^b_4)/N(m_0). B.27: 'A(n,2) = Σ_{*=a,b,c}' should be *=a,c,e, and nA(n,1)/2 should be (n−1)A(n,1)/2. Read literally, the n version does not contradict at n = 5 (65 + 5 + 1 = 71 > 66 = A(5,2)); with n−1 the sum is 58 < 66. B.28 proof: 'For w ≤ q ≤ w+r−1' should be 0 ≤ q ≤ r−1. B.29: the middle term '(dA(n,r−1))(dA(n,r−1)−1)m_H(w−r)/(2d(m_H(w)−m_0(w)+1))' divides by d twice, since m_H(w)−m_0(w)+1 = d; the correct value is A(n,r−1)(dA(n,r−1)−1)m_H(w−r)/2, which gives the stated bound.

findings.claim: All four cited declarations exist at 082e2d3 and say what the note says, so the status 'library' stands. But the list does not back the statement. The statement claims 'recursion and monotonicity' and 'the elementary inequalities used in the combinatorial appendices'. The review labels Nat.add_one_mul_choose_eq 'the recurrence', but it is the absorption identity, not Pascal's rule. The identity the appendices actually use, in every N(m^*)/N(m_0) computation, is the ratio of consecutive binomial coefficients, and it is not cited. Nor are Appendix C's exp/log bounds. 'These are the only library-level ingredients of the appendices' is also inaccurate: Appendix A also needs log-concavity, which is missing (see the finding on cited inputs).

The pairs are /40 ↔ /adjoint-hodge-numbers, /45 ↔ /padic-transcendence, /50 ↔ /induced-filtration, /51 ↔ /balanced-filtrations, /55 ↔ /prop-11-3, and /61 (Lemmas A.2–A.3) ↔ /eulerian-statistics. make_queue.py merges both proposals into one design job (DESIGN-MordellLawrenceVenkateshPartII), so there is no second owner. But brief 1 does not say that LV's statements are the connected special cases, and the two proposals give the same roadmap id different subtitles. Also: Three notions of this extraction are also items of PAPER-LAWRENCE-VENKATESH-20, both routed into the same MordellLawrenceVenkateshPartII. /40 (adjoint Hodge numbers and T) appears there as /adjoint-hodge-numbers, /38 (G-filtrations by cocharacters) as /reductive-filtrations, and /39's Tannakian comparison of fibre functors as /fibre-functor-comparison (MC.6 torsors). LV-20's route 1 says it coalesces with the LS Part II, but the LS items name no counterpart, so the design will receive each notion twice with different statements. LS /40 is the LV notion for a general reductive group with a filtration, and is the more general of the two.
